Ticket: Set up the environment and settings
Acceptance Criteria: The .venv builds from requirements.txt with no errors. config.from_args returns the default settings, or the quick ones with --quick (results go to results_quick/). The tok and base_hf fixtures in tests/conftest.py load GPT-2. Details: Anyone on the team can go from a fresh copy of the repo to a working Python environment by following the README, on the machines the team actually uses, without fixing anything by hand. config.from_args is how every script gets its settings: with no flags it returns the defaults, with --quick it returns the small smoke-test settings and sends output to results_quick/, and --results-dir changes the output folder. The tok and base_hf test fixtures load the real GPT-2 tokenizer and model, so later tests can rely on them. This is done when someone other than the author has repeated the setup successfully.
Notes: File: config.py. Keep the version pins (numpy<2, pyarrow<21, datasets<4); newer versions clash with each other.
Dependencies: None

Ticket: Build the IOI test sentences and their twins
Acceptance Criteria: make_ioi creates 8 prompts per template (120 total) from Wang et al.'s 15 templates, each with a flipped twin and an ABC twin. The first 5 tests in tests/test_tasks.py pass. Details: We need the same 120 sentences at every setting, so they are generated from a seed and never written by hand. Each sentence is a name-completion task like "Sarah and Tom went to the shop. Sarah gave a drink to", where the right answer is the name mentioned once. Prompts alternate between the two name orders (ABBA and BABA). Each prompt gets two twins: the flipped twin swaps only the second mention of the subject so the right answer changes, and the ABC twin puts three fresh, different names in the name slots so there is no right answer to find. Every name, place and object must be exactly one GPT-2 token, so a prompt and its twins line up token for token. The same seed must give identical output, a different seed must give different output, and the positions of the key tokens must be recorded for each prompt.
Notes: File: tasks.py. Also fill the data fixture in conftest.py. Placeholders already have a space before them, so fill them with bare words or you get double spaces. Pad with token 50256.
Dependencies: Set up the environment and settings

Acceptance Criteria: make_induction returns [BOS, A, A] sequences and a [BOS, A, B] corrupt twin from a seed. test_induction_repeats passes. Details: These sequences test the model's copying behaviour. Each one starts with the BOS token, then a block of random tokens (A), then the same block again. A working model should find the second copy much easier to predict than the first. Each sequence also has a corrupt twin with the same first block, followed by a fresh random block (B) that repeats nothing. By default there are 32 sequences with blocks of 50 tokens, and the same seed must always give the same sequences.
Notes: File: tasks.py. Also fill the ind fixture in conftest.py. Small ticket, good first one.
Dependencies: Set up the environment and settings

Ticket: Write the IOI circuit watch list
Acceptance Criteria: IOI_CIRCUIT lists Wang et al.'s 26 heads in 7 classes. KEEP_POSITION gives each class its position. heads_of returns 26 heads. random_heads returns the same 26 non-circuit heads for the same seed. Details: This is the single place in the code that says which heads make up the IOI circuit, so head numbers never get copied into other files. The list needs 3 name movers, 8 backup name movers, 2 negative name movers, 4 S-inhibition heads, 4 induction heads, 3 duplicate-token heads and 2 previous-token heads. Each class also needs the sentence position where it does its job (end, S2 or S1+1). heads_of returns one flat, sorted list with no duplicates. random_heads gives a control group of the requested size from outside the circuit, and repeats exactly for the same seed. A second person must check every head number against the source, because a wrong number here would quietly affect every later result.
Notes: File: circuits.py. Copy heads from the paper / ARENA and have someone double-check every one.
Dependencies: Set up the environment and settings

Ticket: Build the basic rounder (RTN, all weights)
Acceptance Criteria: rtn, quantize_hf (scope "all"), load_tl and build_model work. test_rtn_error_and_levels, test_rtn_16_bits_is_near_identity, test_none_bits_is_untouched and test_only_block_linears_change pass. Details: This is the one thing the project changes between runs. rtn rounds each output channel of a weight matrix to a symmetric grid of 2^bits - 1 levels, and no weight may move by more than half a grid step. Only the linear layers inside the transformer blocks are rounded; embeddings, LayerNorms and biases stay exactly as they were. With bits set to None the model comes back unchanged, and 16-bit rounding should barely change anything. Rounding always works on a fresh copy, so the original model is never altered, and it happens on the Hugging Face weights before the model is loaded into TransformerLens. build_model is the one call the sweep uses to get a ready-to-measure model.
Notes: File: quantize.py. Also fill the fp_model fixture. Round the Hugging Face weights BEFORE loading into TransformerLens, because TransformerLens changes the weights on load.
Dependencies: Set up the environment and settings

Acceptance Criteria: Rounding can target the circuit only, everything except the circuit, or 26 random heads, and can use matched noise or sign-flipped error instead. test_scopes_partition_all, test_random_heads_scope_is_size_matched and test_controls_match_error_size pass. Details: This lets us ask where damage comes from and whether rounding itself matters. head_masks works out which weight entries belong to which heads. Circuit-only and everything-except-circuit must change completely separate entries that together add up to exactly what scope "all" changes. The random-heads scope must change within 5% as many entries as the IOI circuit scope. The noise control adds Gaussian error with the same per-channel size as rounding, and the sign-flip control uses the real rounding error with random signs. Grid scales always come from the whole matrix, and only selected entries change. The code spec also lists circuit and rest scopes for the induction circuit, and those need the saved heads from the induction selection ticket.
Notes: After: basic rounder, IOI watch list. Scales always come from the full matrix; a mask then picks which entries change.
Dependencies: Build the basic rounder (RTN, all weights); Write the IOI circuit watch list; Select the induction circuit from FP32 scores

Acceptance Criteria: load_ppl_windows downloads and caches 16,384 WikiText-2 test tokens. FP32 GPT-2 small scores a perplexity of about 30.8. Details: This is the outside view: the kind of score a company would check before shipping. load_ppl_windows takes the first 16,384 tokens of the WikiText-2 test set and cuts them into non-overlapping windows of 1,024 tokens. The result is cached in the data folder, so the download happens only once. window_losses gives the average next-token loss for each window, and perplexity is the exponential of the mean of those losses. On the uncompressed model the result should be about 30.8, matching the pilot's 30.81. A much different number means the data or the calculation is wrong.
Notes: File: metrics.py. Pilot FP32 value: 30.81.
Dependencies: Build the basic rounder (RTN, all weights)

Acceptance Criteria: logit_diff, ioi_behaviour and induction_logprob work. On FP32: IOI logit diff in [3.0, 4.2], accuracy > 0.9, and the repeated half is > 5 nats easier than the first half. Details: These scores show whether the model still does each task. The logit difference is how much more the model prefers the right name than the wrong one, read at each prompt's own last real token rather than in the padding. ioi_behaviour returns four values for every prompt: the logit difference, whether it is positive, whether the right name is the model's top guess, and the probability of the right name. Values stay per prompt so confidence intervals can be calculated later. induction_logprob reports how well the model predicts the next token in the repeated half and the first half of each sequence. On the uncompressed model, all the target ranges in the acceptance criteria must be met.
Notes: Pilot FP32: logit diff 3.57, accuracy 99%. Read each prompt at its own last real token (pos "end"), not the last column, because prompts are padded.
Dependencies: Build the IOI test sentences and their twins; Build the repeated-token (induction) sequences; Build the basic rounder (RTN, all weights)

Ticket: Select the induction circuit from FP32 scores
Acceptance Criteria: induction_scores prints all 144 heads' scores. The threshold sits in the clear gap between real induction heads and the rest. The chosen heads save to results/induction_heads.json and reload identically. Details: We pick the induction circuit from data, using the uncompressed model only. The induction score measures how much a head looks at the token after an earlier copy of the current token, and the previous-token score measures how much it looks one position back. Print the scores for all 144 heads and set the induction cutoff in the clear gap between real induction heads and other heads. Previous-token heads must pass their own cutoff, sit in a layer before the deepest induction head, and not already count as induction heads. Selection happens once and is saved, so every condition watches the same heads and nothing is reselected on a rounded model. Record the chosen cutoffs and why they were picked.
Notes: After: basic rounder. Pilot picked induction heads 5.1, 5.5, 6.9, 7.2, 7.10 at threshold 0.7. IOI name movers also score ~0.5 on repeated text, so 0.4 is too low.
Dependencies: Build the repeated-token (induction) sequences; Build the basic rounder (RTN, all weights)

Acceptance Criteria: direct_logit_attribution, attention_to, class_sums and cosine_per_head work. On FP32, at least 2 of 9.6, 9.9, 10.0 are in the top-3 positive direct effect, and 10.7 or 11.10 is in the top-3 negative. Details: These measurements show what each head is doing. Direct logit attribution measures how much one head pushes the model towards the right name, one value per head per prompt. attention_to shows how much the last position looks at a chosen part of the sentence. class_sums adds up the direct effect for each class of the circuit, prompt by prompt. cosine_per_head compares each head's output between two models, so a model compared with itself must score 1. On the uncompressed model, the name movers should show up as the strongest positive heads and a negative name mover as one of the strongest negative heads. This is a quick sign that the measurement agrees with the published work.
Notes: Divide by the final LayerNorm scale before dotting with W_U[IO] - W_U[S].
Dependencies: Write the IOI circuit watch list; IOI and copying (induction) behaviour scores

Acceptance Criteria: template_means, keep_mask and the ablation hooks work. Keep-everything leaves the logits unchanged, the keep-mask test passes, and FP32 faithfulness is in [0.70, 1.05]. Details: Faithfulness asks whether the circuit can do the task with almost everything else switched off. A head is switched off by replacing its output with an average taken from the ABC twins of the same template, which contain no IOI signal. Circuit heads keep their real output only at their class's position, and every other head is averaged out everywhere. Faithfulness is the logit difference in this reduced model divided by the normal logit difference. If nothing is switched off, the logits must not change. With the full circuit kept, exactly 26 heads x N prompts entries are marked as kept. The gate also needs a self-repair check built with the same tools, using ablate_heads_mask: switch off the 3 name movers and confirm that the backup name movers increase their contribution.
Notes: Pilot FP32 faithfulness: 0.85 (Wang: ~0.87). Means come from the ABC twins, per template. Circuit heads keep their real output only at their class's position.
Dependencies: Write the IOI circuit watch list; IOI and copying (induction) behaviour scores

Acceptance Criteria: run_with_heads_patched, end_logit_diff and head_patch_map work. All of tests/test_patching.py passes, including the fast map matching TransformerLens within 1e-4. Details: This is the core causal measurement and the main thing that sets the project apart from earlier work. We run the model on the corrupted prompt, copy chosen heads' outputs in from the clean run, and measure how much of the right answer comes back. A recovery of 0 means no better than corrupted, and 1 means fully clean. Clean and corrupted runs always use the same rounded model. Patching nothing must leave the corrupted output exactly as it was, and patching every head from a clean run into itself must return the clean output. head_patch_map does this for all 144 heads one at a time, and must match the slow TransformerLens reference within 1e-4 while running noticeably faster. Two tests in test_patching.py belong to the mean ablation ticket, so that ticket must be finished before this one can fully pass.
Notes: File: patching.py. The TransformerLens version takes ~130 s per model. Speed-up: restart each run at the patched head's own layer (start_at_layer).
Dependencies: IOI and copying (induction) behaviour scores; Mean ablation and faithfulness

Acceptance Criteria: run_sweep.py --quick finishes and writes summary.json, prompts.csv and heads.csv per condition. Rerunning skips finished conditions. The full run produces 49 conditions. Details: This is the one script that runs every experiment in the same way, so nothing depends on settings typed by hand. It covers setup, measure_condition (which gathers every measurement for one model) and the loop itself. The 49 conditions are the uncompressed reference plus 8 variants at each of 6 bit-widths: 3 controls at scope all, and 5 other scopes with normal rounding. Each condition gets a freshly rounded model and writes its three output files, with summary.json written last as the sign that the condition finished. If a run is stopped and restarted, finished conditions are skipped and unfinished ones run again. The induction circuit is selected once and reused, and result names must match what analyze.py reads. The quick run is only a test of the plumbing, and the full 49-condition run must wait until the gate passes.
Notes: File: run_sweep.py. Result names must match the list in measure_condition's docstring, because analyze.py reads them. Full run ~30 min on an M4 laptop.
Dependencies: Add scopes and noise controls; Perplexity benchmark; Per-head readouts (direct effect, attention, cosine); Activation patching and the 144-head map; The gate: checks.py (full run only)

Acceptance Criteria: checks.py prints 15/15 PASS on the uncompressed model, writes results/checks.json, and exits with an error if any check fails. Details: The gate proves our measuring tools are right before we trust any compressed result. Part A checks that the uncompressed model reproduces published results: aligned twins, logit difference, accuracy, name-mover rankings, faithfulness, self-repair and induction behaviour. Part B checks that the pipeline invents nothing: our model loading matches the standard loader, comparing the uncompressed model with itself reports no change, and 16-bit rounding moves every summary metric by less than 0.5%. Each check prints one PASS or FAIL line with its detail, and all results are saved to results/checks.json. Any failure makes the script exit with an error, so it cannot be missed. If a threshold ever has to change, the reason must be written down at the time.
Notes: Nothing gets compressed until this passes. Never loosen a threshold without writing down why.
Dependencies: The sweep loop (measure_condition only)

Ticket: Normalize results and add confidence intervals
Acceptance Criteria: normalized.csv has every metric for every condition as a fraction of FP32, with 95% bootstrap CIs. FP32 rows equal 1.00 and 16-bit rows are within 0.5% of 1. Details: This turns raw sweep output into comparable numbers. Every metric is divided by its uncompressed value, so 1.0 means unchanged and lower generally means worse. Perplexity is inverted first, so its ratio reads as a fraction of uncompressed quality. Each value gets a 95% confidence interval from 1,000 bootstrap resamples, using the same resampled prompts for the condition and for the uncompressed model. The random seed is fixed, so re-running gives the same table. The analysis reads only the raw results, so it can be repeated without re-running the sweep. The output needs one row per condition and metric, with the bit-width, scope, control, level, value and interval.
Notes: File: analyze.py. Paired bootstrap: resample the same prompts for the condition and for FP32.
Dependencies: The sweep loop

Acceptance Criteria: analyze.py saves the 6 figures and a summary.txt that answers H1, H2 and H3 with numbers. No overlapping labels on any figure. Details: This is where the numbers become the finding. The six figures show: benchmark vs behaviour vs circuit metrics, whether backup heads take over, whether damage is local or inherited, rounding vs matched noise and sign-flipped error, geometry vs causality, and the 144-head maps. summary.txt must include the metric table, where each metric first crosses the 0.95, 0.9 and 0.8 thresholds, and a direct answer on each hypothesis with supporting numbers. H1 asks for precisions where a circuit metric is below 0.9 while perplexity stays at 0.9 or higher. H2 asks which circuit breaks first. H3 compares damage from rounding the whole model, only the circuit, everything except the circuit, and random heads. A result against a hypothesis must be reported just as plainly as a result for it. Every figure must be readable without overlapping labels.
Notes: Use the palette at the top of analyze.py. Hypotheses are in PREDICTIONS.md.
Dependencies: Normalize results and add confidence intervals

Acceptance Criteria: A full run of the new code matches the pilot's summary numbers to 2 decimal places (e.g. 4-bit: perplexity 48.1, logit diff 1.68, accuracy 79%). Details: This confirms the rebuilt code gives the same answers as the working pilot. Run the full sweep and analysis, then compare the new summary numbers with the pilot's across the conditions, not just the 4-bit examples. Keep a short written comparison showing what matched and what did not. Any difference must be traced to its cause before moving on. A difference could be a bug in the new code or a bug in the pilot, so a mismatch should be explained rather than simply forced to agree. Everyone working on this ticket needs access to the pilot results, and exact matches will need the same test prompts as the pilot.
Notes: Pilot results: ~/Desktop/I.N.T.A.C.T_pilot_backup_2026-11-05/results. If anything differs, find out why before moving on.
Dependencies: The gate: checks.py; Figures 1-6 and summary.txt

Ticket: Repeat each setting with several rounding draws
Acceptance Criteria: Every rounded condition runs with 5 seeded random rounding draws (stochastic rounding), and every figure shows the spread across draws instead of one number. Details: One run per setting cannot show how much a result depends on chance. Each rounded condition is repeated 5 times with stochastic rounding, where the seed decides each draw so any run can be repeated exactly. Figures and tables then show the spread across the draws as well as the central value. The results should say whether odd patterns, such as circuit-only rounding scoring higher at 3 bits than at 4 bits, go away or persist. Stochastic results must be clearly labelled, so they are not confused with the pilot's RTN numbers. This should be finished before any result is claimed.
Notes: Pilot had one draw per setting. Circuit-only rounding scored higher at 3 bits (3.56) than at 4 bits (3.25), probably luck. Do this before claiming any result.
Dependencies: Match the pilot's numbers

Ticket: Find where the damage comes from
Acceptance Criteria: At 4 bits, round everything except one component at a time (each of the 12 MLP layers and 12 attention layers). A chart shows how much IOI logit diff each protected component brings back and names the top 3. Details: This narrows down which parts of the model cause the damage. Starting from a fully rounded 4-bit model, each run protects one component and rounds everything else, giving 24 runs: 12 MLP layers and 12 attention layers. A component's score is how much logit difference it brings back compared with the fully rounded model. New scope names are needed in quantize.py, with tests confirming that the protected weights stay exact and all the others are rounded. The chart ranks the 24 components, shows uncertainty, and names the top 3. If no component clearly stands out, that is a valid result and must be reported as such.
Notes: Pilot: protecting the 26 circuit heads only raised logit diff from 1.68 to 1.92, so most damage is outside the circuit. Needs new scope names in quantize.py.
Dependencies: Repeat each setting with several rounding draws

Acceptance Criteria: At least 3 difficulty levels (more names, names further apart, distracting sentences). Each level reports the 16-bit vs 4-bit gap with CIs. Details: Normal IOI sentences may be too easy to reveal damage. Build at least 3 harder prompt sets, for example with more names, names further apart, or distracting sentences, all generated from a seed like the originals. Run each set on the 16-bit and 4-bit models and report the gap between them with confidence intervals. First confirm the near-uncompressed model still does each harder task reasonably well, because a task that is already failing can't show further damage. The conclusion should say whether the gap grows as the prompts get harder.
Notes: Tests whether benchmarks hide damage on hard cases. Only needs new prompt generators in tasks.py.
Dependencies: Repeat each setting with several rounding draws

Acceptance Criteria: A GPTQ-rounded model at 4 and 3 bits runs through the same pipeline and is compared with RTN at the same bits. Details: RTN is simple but is not how most people's 4-bit models are made. This ticket adds GPTQ, a smarter method, and checks whether our findings still hold with it. Build GPTQ models at 4 and 3 bits and measure them with the same pipeline and the same uncompressed reference. Present the results beside RTN at the same bit-widths, including perplexity, behaviour and circuit metrics. GPTQ needs calibration data, so say what was used and keep it separate from the test prompts. If any part of the pipeline can't apply to GPTQ, state which part and why.
Notes: The 4-bit files people download use smarter rounding (GPTQ, Q4_K_M). RTN is the worst case, so this checks the result holds in practice.
Dependencies: Repeat each setting with several rounding draws

Ticket: Cheap repair: keep the culprits at 8 bits
Acceptance Criteria: Keeping only the culprit components at 8 bits (rest at 4) reports % extra model size vs % IOI logit diff recovered. Details: If a few parts cause most of the damage, keeping only those parts at higher precision could be a cheap fix. Using the top components from the damage ticket, build a model with those at 8 bits and everything else at 4 bits. Report the percentage of extra model size compared with a model at 4 bits throughout, with the size calculation written down. Report recovery as the share of lost IOI logit difference that comes back, measured between the 4-bit and uncompressed models. The headline in the notes is a hope, not a target, so the ticket is done whether or not the fix works, as long as the trade-off is measured honestly.
Notes: After: Find where the damage comes from. Headline if it works: "protect ~5% of weights, recover ~90%".
Dependencies: Find where the damage comes from

Acceptance Criteria: Every cited paper has a correct arXiv link, and what we say about it matches the paper. Details: Several references were written from memory and may be wrong. For every paper we cite, including those in the notes, someone must find the real paper, confirm the title, authors, year and link, and read enough of it to check what we say. Any number quoted from a paper must match the source. A claim that can't be confirmed must be corrected or removed. Keep a simple checklist showing who verified each citation.
Notes: Written from memory, must verify: Zhang 2024 (quantization undoes unlearning), Arditi 2024 (refusal direction), Egashira 2024 (exploiting quantization), the "super weights" paper.
Dependencies: None

Acceptance Criteria: A workshop-length draft (intro, method, results with figures, limits) that the whole team has read. Details: Write a complete draft that an outside reader could follow, rather than an outline. It covers why the question matters, how we measured it, what we found, and where the work is limited. Every number and figure must trace back to saved results, and hypotheses the results did not support must be reported as such. Everyone on the team must have read it and confirmed they stand behind it. The target is roughly 22 December 2026 to 22 January 2027, based on 2-3 months from October 22.
Notes: Main claim depends on: Repeat each setting, Find where the damage comes from. Goal: ~2-3 months from Oct 22, 2026.
Dependencies: Figures 1-6 and summary.txt; Repeat each setting with several rounding draws; Find where the damage comes from; Check every citation

Acceptance Criteria: The pipeline runs on Pythia-160M with its IOI circuit located and the gate adapted. Details: A finding that holds on only one model might be a quirk of that model. This ticket runs the same study on Pythia-160M. Its weight layout and head numbers differ from GPT-2's, so the rounder must be adapted and the circuit found again rather than copied. The gate needs Pythia versions of its checks, and any changed threshold must be justified in writing. It's done when Pythia passes its gate and produces results that can be compared with GPT-2's.
Notes: Also unlocks "Does compression rewind training?" using Pythia's saved checkpoints.
Dependencies: Match the pilot's numbers

Acceptance Criteria: 4-bit Pythia's IOI behaviour is matched to the closest training checkpoint, with a chart. Details: The pilot hints that a 4-bit model makes the same kinds of mistakes as a less-trained model. To test this, measure IOI behaviour at Pythia's saved training checkpoints, then find which checkpoint looks most like the 4-bit model. Decide how similarity will be measured before looking at the match. The chart should show the checkpoints over training with the 4-bit model marked against them. The result must also say how close the match really is, because a closest checkpoint always exists even if the idea is wrong.
Notes: After: Pythia. Pilot hint: 4-bit mistakes look like an undertrained model's (it picks the repeated name).
Dependencies: Second model family (Pythia)

Acceptance Criteria: Report whether DistilGPT2 does IOI and whether it uses the same kind of heads (patching map vs GPT-2's). Details: DistilGPT2 is a smaller model made by compressing what a larger model learned, which is a different kind of compression from rounding. First measure whether it can do the IOI task at all. If it can, build its patching map and put it beside GPT-2's to see whether it relies on the same kinds of heads. If it can't, report that clearly and stop. The report should answer both questions directly, and treat any claim that it gets the answer without the circuit with care.
Notes: “Gets the answer without the circuit” would be a strong result.
Dependencies: Match the pilot's numbers

Ticket: More circuits: do longer circuits break first?
Acceptance Criteria: 3+ more known tasks (e.g. greater-than, acronyms, pronouns) measured across bits, with a chart of breaking point vs circuit length. Details: With only two circuits we can't say whether circuit length affects fragility. This ticket adds at least 3 more known tasks, such as greater-than, acronyms and pronouns. Each one needs seeded prompts, a behaviour measure, and a check that the uncompressed model does the task. Measure each across the same bit-widths and use the same definition of breaking for all of them. Write down how circuit length is defined before seeing the results. The chart plots breaking point against length, and the conclusion should reflect how few circuits it rests on.
Notes: Pilot hint: IOI (~7 steps) dropped at 5 bits; induction (2 steps) held until 4.
Dependencies: Match the pilot's numbers

Ticket: Canary prompts to detect silent quantization
Acceptance Criteria: A set of 50 or fewer prompts tells 5-bit from 16-bit using only output probabilities, more reliably than perplexity. Details: Users of an API can't see how compressed the model behind it is. This ticket looks for a short set of test prompts, 50 or fewer, that can reveal this using only the probabilities the model returns. The test must tell a 5-bit model from a 16-bit model, and do so more reliably than perplexity. Choose the prompts on one set of data and measure their success on separate data, so the score isn't inflated. Report how often the test gets it right, and spell out how it was compared with perplexity.
Notes: The API angle: users can't see the bits behind an API.
Dependencies: Match the pilot's numbers
